articles.author: Elarigent
articles.description:
Twenty-eight articles in, one pattern keeps showing up. Owners do not ask for more AI. They do not ask for a bigger model, a smarter chatbot, or a longer list of features. They ask one plain question, in three parts: what does it do, what does it touch, and who approves? This morning's post asked which of the two matters more to you — what it does, or who approves. After 28 days of writing about this gap, the honest answer is that the question is a trap, and the trap is the point: the doing is worthless without the approving, and the approving is pointless without the doing.
This article was drafted with AI assistance. It is written in plain English for people who run businesses, not for people who build software, and it makes no claim about any particular product. Yesterday's article — ht…
articles.title: What It Does, or Who Approves? The One Question Every Owner Asks First

articles.author: MergedCode
articles.description:
It's easy to get addicted to the dopamine loop of Jira tickets moving to 'Done'.
You ship feature after feature, close ticket after ticket, and rack up sprint points. But if your health is degrading, your friendships are fading, and you haven't taken a walk in daylight for a week, what are you actually winning?
The sprint board never empties. There will always be another ticket waiting for you.
Ship your work, but make sure you have a real life waiting when you shut the lid.
Build a life, not just a backlog.


  
  
  WorkLifeBalance #DeveloperLife #CareerAdvice #Burnout #MergedCode

articles.author: Sten Roger Sandvik
articles.description:
Stagd signs people in with a code by email. People who review previews, such as designers, product managers and clients, often have no GitHub account, so the code is how they get in. It has one job: arrive within a minute, in the inbox.
At a Gmail address it did. At a Microsoft 365 address it went to Junk, or didn't show up at all. This is how we found out why, and why the usual checklist wasn't the answer.
When mail goes to spam, the first suspects are always the same three records, so we checked them first:
SPF: passed, through the bounce domain our sending service uses.
DKIM: passed, signed for our own domain.
DMARC: passed, with a p=reject policy, the strictest there is.
Microsoft agreed. The headers of a junked code said so in its own words:
spf=pass  dkim=pass header.d=stagd-staging.…
articles.title: Our sign-in codes went to Junk, and every check passed

articles.author: Marius Podar
articles.description:
La sesión de PHP es donde vive el «he iniciado sesión como este usuario», así que si está mal configurada puede convertirse en un punto débil: quien consiga manipularla puede suplantar a otra persona sin conocer su contraseña. Aquí repasamos cómo configurar sesiones seguras en PHP: cookies bien configuradas, regeneración del ID tras el login y qué conviene evitar guardar dentro de la sesión.
Dos ataques clásicos aprovechan sesiones mal configuradas:
Session fixation: el atacante fuerza a la víctima a usar un ID de sesión que él ya conoce, por ejemplo mediante un enlace. Cuando la víctima inicia sesión, el atacante usa ese mismo ID para entrar como ella.
Session hijacking: el atacante roba una cookie de sesión ya activa, por ejemplo interceptando tráfico sin HTTPS o mediante XSS, y la usa d…
articles.title: Sesiones seguras en PHP: cookies, regenerar el ID y logout (guía rápida)

articles.author: Mohamed Elgohary
articles.description:
The car on a ride-hailing map is not where the driver is. It is where the app guesses the driver is.
The driver's phone reports a GPS position every few seconds, not continuously. If the rider's app drew each report the moment it arrived, the car would teleport from point to point. So the app animates the car from one report toward the next, and the animation is invented. Most of the time the invention is good. Sometimes the car takes a strange turn, cuts through a building and snaps back to the road. The guess was off, and the next real position corrected it.
I don't know how Uber, Careem or any other app implements this, and each one tunes its own details. This article describes the general pattern and one way to build it in Kotlin with Flow, including the numbers you have to choose and …
articles.title: The car on your ride-hailing map is a guess

Over the past few weeks I compared how different platforms give AI agents "business context" — the definitions, metrics, relationships and rules an agent needs to answer questions about company data correctly. I looked at Databricks Genie Ontology, Palantir Ontology, Microsoft Fabric IQ and Foundry IQ, Snowflake Semantic Views, AWS Context, Google Knowledge Catalog, and graph tools like Neo4j and Stardog.
Here's what stuck with me, independent of which vendor you pick.
Some products model the business explicitly (objects, links, actions). Some describe metrics and dimensions for SQL. Some retrieve documents for agents. Before comparing features, decide which of those three problems you actually have.
Explicit modeling gives you precision and control, but someone has to build and maintain i…

articles.author: Zhou Jia
articles.description:
If your site is built from templates, there is a good chance every page in your sitemap has the same lastmod date — the date of your last deploy.
That is not a lie you tell on purpose. It falls out of the build: a footer change touches all 1,287 files, the generator stamps each one with now(), and the sitemap faithfully reports that the entire site changed at 14:32 on Tuesday.
To a crawler, that means: nothing here is more important than anything else. So it re-checks everything, in whatever order it feels like, and the pages you actually care about wait in the same queue as the ones nobody will ever link to.
I had exactly this. Search Console told me 51% of my crawl budget was going to Refresh and 49% to Discovery, with 299 pages sitting in Discovered - currently not indexed.
The fix is n…
articles.title: Your sitemap lastmod Is Lying. Here's a 40-Line Fix That Made Mine Honest

articles.author: Mediatavio
articles.description:
An outdoor interview can contain traffic, footsteps and wind on the microphone at the same time. The useful question is not whether every pause can become silent. It is whether the conversation becomes easier to understand without changing the words or making the voice unstable.
Keep the original recording and edit a copy. Note where the important answers occur before processing. One setting may work for a calm passage but damage a quieter answer recorded just after a gust.
Steady hiss and distant environmental noise differ from bursts of air striking a microphone. Wind may create very low-frequency energy or overload the recording. Speech denoising can reduce some unwanted sound, but is not a reliable repair for clipped audio or missing syllables.
Listen to the speaker's softest words as …
articles.title: How to Reduce Wind Noise in an Outdoor Interview Recording
